sections.h2: Who sends and collects the tax bill
sections.html:
Nash County runs assessing and collecting out of one combined office. It lists and values real and personal property, assesses it, and collects the tax. The office is at 120 W. Washington St., Suite 2058, Nashville, NC 27856, and the phone is 252-459-9824 during business hours, eight in the morning to five.

Relief applications under state law go through this office too. The collector handles payments, while questions about listing, billing and assessed values belong with the assessor's staff, so call the right desk for the right question.

The county commissioners set the rate in spring, by June 30 at the latest, and the bill multiplies that rate by each $100 of taxable value. Bills go out in July or August. If you have no statement by September 15, call the collector.

sections.h2: Nash County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Nash County has about 99,365 residents as of mid-2025, up 4.6% from 2020. The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $191,000, and 63.6% of households own their home. Typical rent runs $953 a month, and the county has 45,068 homes and apartments.

Because roughly a third of households rent, plenty of Nash County houses are investor-owned. A landlord selling should remember that the county bills whoever held title on January 1, whatever the tenant pays.

The bill is due September 1, and you can pay without interest through January 5. If January 5 lands on a weekend, payment is accepted through the next working day. A postmark on or before the cutoff counts, and the county suggests mailing a full week early.

Real estate and personal property accounts left unpaid are charged 2% for January, then 0.75% every month after, per G.S. 105-360. Registered vehicles follow their own rule: 5% in the first month past due.

  • Delinquent real estate may be advertised in local papers between March 1 and June 30, with the cost charged to the owner.
  • Collection tools include wage garnishment, attachment of bank accounts or rents, foreclosure, and offsets against state income tax refunds.
  • Prepayments toward a coming bill are accepted, and staff can explain the terms.

A seller stays liable for the year's bill. The legal obligation sits with whoever held title on January 1, and a later sale does not wipe it out.

Proration normally happens at closing, so confirm with your agent or closing attorney that it did. For certainty, you can direct a check to the Tax Collector's Office from the closing table. If the current bill is not yet due, the collector takes a prepayment computed at last year's rate.

Under G.S. 105-355, the tax lien attaches to the parcel on the listing date, and no buyer or lender will accept title with it open. Once you have a closing date, ask the county tax office to put the amount owed in writing and bring that letter to the closing attorney.

A cash buyer can usually close faster and skip the lender's payoff and escrow steps, but the tax still has to be settled from the proceeds or prorated.

An informal appeal comes first. Only if that fails does the dispute reach the county review board, and no taxpayer may skip a step, as the county's revaluation page spells out.

The informal step can be started four ways.

  • By appointment, face to face with an appraiser at the West Washington Street office in Nashville.
  • Over the phone, once an appraiser agrees to call you back.
  • By mail: fill in the bottom of the appeal notice and send it with your documents to the Tax Office, marked for the Board of Equalization and Review.
  • Online, using the county's informal appeal form.

After the informal answer arrives, you have thirty days from the notice date to go formal, and you must prove the value is wrong. Under G.S. 105-322 the board's opening session falls in a spring window, April into early May.

The board looks only at whether the value is fair and accurate, not at whether the tax is affordable. Your best exhibit is a set of similar nearby homes assessed lower. If the board says no, the next stop is the Property Tax Commission, and written notice is due a month after the ruling is mailed (G.S. 105-290).

Nash County offers four: the elderly and permanently disabled exclusion, the disabled veteran exclusion, the circuit breaker deferment and the builder's inventory exclusion. Request an application at (252) 459-1222 or download one from the tax forms page.

Elderly or disabled, disabled veteran, circuit breakerApplication due June 1

For 2026 the income limit is $38,800 for the elderly or disabled exclusion and circuit breaker, with $58,200 as the ceiling for the higher circuit breaker tier. Under the elderly or disabled exclusion, the larger of a flat $25,000 or half the home's appraised value comes off the assessment (G.S. 105-277.1). A disabled veteran can exclude $45,000 of value regardless of age or income.

Reappraisals can be no more than eight years apart under state law, each taking effect January 1 of its scheduled year (G.S. 105-286). Nash County says the goal is a fair and accurate value on every parcel.

The current project covers more than 53,000 parcels and is carried out with an outside firm, Piner Appraisal, whose appraisers also take informal appeals. Each owner is mailed the new assessed value, and the thirty days run from the date on that notice.

Market value here means what a willing buyer and seller would agree on with no pressure on either side, so foreclosure and family sales do not count. If your own sale was one of those, bring different comparables.

sections.h2: Other items the tax office handles
sections.html:
The collector's side of the office also deals with vehicles, business owners and utility customers, which helps when you are closing out a household or a rental.

  • Bills for registered motor vehicles go out monthly instead of in the fall, and they have their own interest rule.
  • Business licenses are issued through the Tax Collector's Office.
  • Personal and business personal property forms must be in the office by the end of January, and a late listing carries a 10% penalty.
  • Check or cash payments for county water and sewer bills can be made at the Tax Collections Office in the administrative building in Nashville during regular business hours.

The Register of Deeds sits in the same administrative building, on the third floor at 120 W. Washington Street, so a seller can record a deed and ask the tax office about a payoff in one trip.

faqs.q: What is the Nash County due date?
faqs.a: September 1 starts the payment period, and it runs through January 5 (extended past a weekend January 5). Interest of 2% then applies for January, followed by 0.75% each month.

faqs.q: If I sell partway through the year, do I still owe that year's tax?
faqs.a: Yes, unless it is settled at closing. The person who held title on January 1 is legally responsible, and a sale does not change that. Proration is typical, or you can pay the Tax Collector directly at the table.

faqs.q: How can I challenge my Nash County assessment?
faqs.a: Begin with an informal appeal, by phone, mail, web form or in person. If the answer disappoints you, file a formal appeal with the Board of Equalization and Review thirty days after the date shown on the informal result.

faqs.q: When must Nash County relief applications arrive?
faqs.a: June 1 is the date for elderly or disabled, disabled veteran, circuit breaker and builders' inventory applications. Classified-parcel exemptions on Form AV-10 are due January 31.

faqs.q: How steep is the Nash County late listing penalty?
faqs.a: It is 10%. Personal and business personal property forms must reach the county by January 31, and late ones carry that penalty.
